chapters.caption: Guildhall — the City of London's seat of government for over 800 years.
chapters.directions: Enter Guildhall Yard; the Great Hall entrance is on the west side of the yard, the Art Gallery on the east.
chapters.text: Welcome to the square mile's front room. Guildhall has been the City of London's centre of government for more than 800 years — and the City, remember, is not quite London as visitors know it. It's the ancient square mile, with its own Lord Mayor, its own police, its own ceremonies and its own government, the City of London Corporation, which still runs this district from this building today. The present Guildhall was begun in 1411, and its Great Hall is the third-largest medieval hall in England. This site has seen everything: Roman London's amphitheatre lies literally beneath your feet, medieval merchants built their power here, a nine-days queen was condemned to death in the hall, and the building has been burned twice — in the Great Fire of 1666 and the Blitz of 1940 — and rebuilt both times, because the City always rebuilds. Our tour is in three movements: the Great Hall and its giants; the Art Gallery across the yard, with its Victorian treasures and one of the biggest paintings in Britain; and then down into the basement, 2,000 years down, to stand in the arena where gladiators fought. Almost everything is free, and on a weekday you'll often have it nearly to yourself — this is one of central London's great under-visited sights. Start in the yard itself, and look at the building's strange, handsome facade: medieval Gothic below, with a quirky 18th-century 'Hindoostani Gothic' porch on top, as if two centuries couldn't agree and decided to share.
chapters.title: Introduction: The City's Ceremonial Heart

chapters.caption: The Great Hall (1411) — London's medieval banqueting and judgement hall, roofed again after fire twice.
chapters.directions: Cross Guildhall Yard to the Art Gallery entrance on the east side.
chapters.text: If the Great Hall is open — it hosts state banquets and City ceremonies, so access varies — step inside and take the measure of it: 46 metres long, with walls a metre and a half thick, built between 1411 and 1440 and still doing the job it was designed for. This is the room where the City governs and feasts. Each autumn the new Lord Mayor is sworn in here in a ceremony conducted, by ancient custom, in complete silence; each year the Prime Minister addresses the Guildhall banquet after the Lord Mayor's Show. But the hall's history has a darker register. In 1553, Lady Jane Grey — queen for nine days — was tried for high treason beneath this roof, and condemned; Henry Garnet, a Gunpowder Plot conspirator, was tried here in 1606. Look along the walls for the monuments: Nelson, Wellington, Pitt the Elder, Churchill, the heroes the City chose to honour in stone, and for the stained-glass windows recording the names of mayors back to the 12th century. Above you, the roof is the hall's third: the medieval original burned in the Great Fire of 1666 — the stone walls, almost alone among the City's buildings, survived — and its replacement burned again in a single night of the Blitz, 29 December 1940. The present timber roof, raised in the 1950s, deliberately echoes the first. A building that has been unroofed by fire twice and simply carried on: that's the City of London in one room.
chapters.title: The Great Hall: Judgement, Banquets and Fire

chapters.caption: Gog and Magog — the nine-foot guardians of the City, watching over the hall from the minstrels' gallery.
chapters.directions: Head back across the yard and into the Guildhall Art Gallery; start with the main Victorian displays on the ground floor.
chapters.text: Before you leave the hall, look up at the west end. Watching over everything from the gallery are two enormous figures, nine feet tall: Gog and Magog, the legendary giant guardians of London. Their story is gloriously murky. In the old foundation myths, Britain was settled by Brutus of Troy, whose companion Corineus wrestled the giant Gogmagog — last of a race of giants — and threw him off a cliff; later storytellers split him into two giants, Gog and Magog, brought in chains to guard the gates of the new city of London. Effigies of the pair have stood in Guildhall since the early 1700s, when wooden statues carved by Richard Saunders were installed as the City's protectors; giant wicker versions of them still process through the streets in the Lord Mayor's Show each November, as they have for centuries. The pair you see today are the third generation: the 1708 originals were destroyed when the hall burned in the Blitz, and these replacements, carved by David Evans, took their place in 1953. There's something touching in that — London burned, and one of the first things the City replaced was its giants. If the Great Hall is closed for an event on your visit, don't despair: you can usually glimpse the giants through the great west window from the yard, standing guard over an empty hall, patient as ever.
chapters.title: Gog and Magog: The Giants Who Guard London

chapters.caption: Inside the Guildhall Art Gallery — the City of London Corporation's collection, strong on Victorian painting.
chapters.directions: Move through the Victorian galleries toward the great Copley canvas, which fills the wall at the gallery's heart.
chapters.text: Cross the yard now to the Guildhall Art Gallery, the City's own gallery since 1885 — though the building you enter, opened in 1999, is the third on this site, its predecessor having been destroyed in the Blitz along with much of the collection. What survives and has been gathered since amounts to over 4,000 works, all belonging to the City of London Corporation, and the gallery's great strength is Victorian painting, hung in rich, dark-walled rooms that suit it perfectly. The Pre-Raphaelites are the draw. Look for Dante Gabriel Rossetti's La Ghirlandata of 1873 — a woman with a harp in a haze of honeysuckle and larkspur, modelled by Christina Rossetti and Alexa Wilding, so drenched in mood it seems to hum. Then find John Everett Millais's much-loved pair, My First Sermon and My Second Sermon (1863–64): the same little girl in the same church pew, first wide-eyed in her new finery, then — the joke lands instantly — fast asleep. They were sensations in their day, reproduced in thousands of Victorian homes. Around them, the collection does what a city gallery should: portraits of Londoners, pageants and processions, the Thames in all weathers, and large-scale history painting of the kind the Victorians adored. The gallery is free, calm and rarely crowded — paintings this good, in peace and quiet, five minutes from the Bank of England.
chapters.title: The Art Gallery: Victorian Highlights

chapters.caption: John Singleton Copley's Defeat of the Floating Batteries at Gibraltar (completed 1791) — Britain's largest oil painting.
chapters.directions: Now find the stairs or lift and descend to the basement level for the Roman Amphitheatre.
chapters.text: You cannot miss the gallery's centrepiece, because it occupies an entire wall and two storeys of the building: John Singleton Copley's The Defeat of the Floating Batteries at Gibraltar, September 1782. At over 42 square metres, it is the largest oil painting in Britain, and the present gallery was literally designed around it. The City commissioned the American-born Copley to celebrate a famous victory of the American Revolutionary War era — not against the Americans, but against Spain and France, whose supposedly unsinkable, fireproof 'floating batteries' attacked Gibraltar during the Great Siege and were destroyed by red-hot shot fired from the Rock's batteries. The canvas is a controlled explosion of smoke, flame and drama: the burning batteries in the harbour, British gun crews at work, and in the foreground the governor, General Eliott, on horseback directing the rescue of drowning Spanish sailors — the humane detail that made the picture's reputation. Stand back as far as the room allows, then go close and pick out individual faces; Copley painted portraits of real officers into the crowd. Before you head downstairs, check whether the small Heritage Gallery is showing the City's treasures — items rotate through it, and they can include the City of London's own 1297 copy of Magna Carta and a property deed bearing one of the six surviving signatures of William Shakespeare. From oil paint to parchment to, next, raw Roman stone.
chapters.title: One Painting, Two Storeys: The Copley Gibraltar Canvas

chapters.caption: London's Roman Amphitheatre, built around AD 70 and lost for nearly 1,900 years until its rediscovery in 1988.
chapters.directions: Return to ground level and step out into Guildhall Yard to see the amphitheatre's outline from above.
chapters.text: Take the lift down, and down, and down through the centuries. In the gallery's basement, in a darkened, atmospheric chamber, you are standing in the eastern entrance and arena wall of London's Roman amphitheatre — the only one the capital ever had. It was built around AD 70, first in timber and later rebuilt in stone in the early 2nd century, and it held about 6,000 spectators: a third of Roman London's entire population could crowd in to watch gladiators fight, wild beasts be hunted, and public executions staged as entertainment. Then Rome fell, the city shrank, and the amphitheatre was so completely forgotten that for nearly 1,900 years Londoners built on top of it without knowing — the medieval Guildhall itself rose almost exactly over the arena. It was rediscovered only in 1988, when archaeologists digging ahead of this gallery's construction found the curved stone walls, the drainage channel that carried away rainwater (and worse), and the timber-lined entrance where the gladiators would have waited in the dark, listening to the crowd. The display is cleverly done: the genuine ragstone walls are lit low, and glowing green outlines complete the missing architecture, with projected figures of gladiators and spectators flickering where the crowd once roared. Stand in the arena entrance for a moment. Above you: Victorian paintings and a medieval hall. Beneath Roman London: you.
chapters.title: The Roman Amphitheatre: Gladiators Under the Gallery

chapters.caption: Guildhall Yard — the amphitheatre's ellipse is traced in dark stone across the paving, with Wren's St Lawrence Jewry on the south side.
chapters.directions: From Guildhall Yard, Bank, St Paul's and Moorgate stations are all within a few minutes' walk.
chapters.text: Finish back up in daylight, in Guildhall Yard — and now look down. Set into the paving in a ring of dark stone is a great ellipse: that is the outline of the amphitheatre below, drawn at full size on the surface of the modern city. Walk its curve and you pace out the arena where the crowds sat in the reign of Trajan; office workers eat their sandwiches on it every lunchtime, which feels exactly right for London, a city that has never let history get in the way of lunch. Take a last look around the yard: the Guildhall's facade to the west, the Art Gallery behind you, and on the south side the elegant church of St Lawrence Jewry, rebuilt by Christopher Wren after the Great Fire and now the official church of the Lord Mayor and Corporation — pop in if it's open; the interior is one of Wren's most richly decorated. And that's our tour: three Londons stacked in one small yard — Roman Londinium's arena at the bottom, the medieval City's hall in the middle, and a working seat of government on top, still electing its Lord Mayor, still processing its giants through the streets each November. Most visitors to London never find this place. You have, and on a quiet day you'll have had 2,000 years of the city almost to yourself. The Bank of England and St Paul's are both five minutes away when you're ready to rejoin the crowds.
chapters.title: Guildhall Yard and Wrap-Up: Three Londons, One Yard

intro: Here's one of London's great secrets, hiding in plain sight in the financial district: the City of London's own ceremonial headquarters, its art gallery, and — underneath both — the remains of a Roman amphitheatre that lay forgotten for 1,900 years. Guildhall has governed the Square Mile for over 800 years, and this compact tour takes you through all three of its layers: the medieval Great Hall with its giant guardians Gog and Magog, a free gallery of Victorian painting built around the largest oil painting in Britain, and then a descent into the basement to stand where gladiators entered the arena. It's free, it's rarely busy, and it packs 2,000 years into about an hour.

location.name: Guildhall, Guildhall Yard, City of London

mapNote: Everything is in and around Guildhall Yard, off Gresham Street. The Great Hall entrance is on the west side of the yard; the Art Gallery is the modern building on the east side, and the Roman Amphitheatre is in its basement (stairs and lift inside the gallery). The amphitheatre's outline is traced in dark stone in the yard's paving between the two. St Lawrence Jewry church stands on the yard's south side.
practical: Guildhall Art Gallery and the Roman Amphitheatre are free; the gallery is generally open Monday–Saturday 10:00–17:00 and Sunday 12:00–16:00, but check the City of London website on the day.
The Great Hall is a working ceremonial space and closes for banquets, elections and private events — access is never guaranteed, so treat entry as a bonus and check ahead if it matters to you.
Nearest Tube stations are Bank, Moorgate and St Paul's, all a few minutes' walk; the City is quietest (and loveliest) at weekends, when the offices are empty.
The amphitheatre is in the gallery's basement with step-free lift access; lighting there is deliberately low and atmospheric.
Photography for personal use is generally allowed in the gallery; the Great Hall has its own rules when events are on.
Combine this visit with the Bank of England Museum (also free, weekdays) and St Paul's Cathedral, both within a short walk.
subtitle: A medieval great hall, giants, Victorian masterpieces — and a Roman amphitheatre in the basement
title: Guildhall Art Gallery & the Roman Amphitheatre
